title: Organisation of learning

blocks.heading: Organisation of learning
blocks.text: Formal education operates within the recognised structured education system; non-formal education is organised outside its main system, while informal learning occurs through everyday experience. The distinction concerns organisation, not quality or whether teaching uses old or new knowledge. An adult course may be non-formal but carefully planned.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Formal education
blocks.text: Formal education is education organised within the recognised, structured education system, normally with planned stages and qualifications. A school course illustrates it. Whether its teaching is effective requires separate evidence about access, learning and support.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Informal education
blocks.text: Informal education is learning through everyday experience and interaction outside a planned education programme. Learning a household repair through daily interaction may illustrate it. Informal does not mean worthless or necessarily inaccurate.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Non-formal education
blocks.text: Non-formal education is organised learning outside the main formal education system, such as a planned adult skills programme. It can fit adult work schedules, but needs suitable teaching and resources. It differs from unplanned everyday learning.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Apply the distinction
blocks.text: Suggest a learning route where invented adult workers need planned tool training outside school and can attend only evenings. Provide a suitable non-formal evening programme with safe practical instruction and resources. It matches the time constraint and need for organised training.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
